evidence.raw_text: LACMUS: Latent Concept Masking for General Robustness Enhancement of DNNs

The susceptibility of Deep Neural Networks (DNNs) to adversarial attacks and their limited robustness to real-world variations pose substantial challenges to their widespread adoption. Adversarial training has shown promise in fortifying models against such perturbations, however current methods are often specific to a single type of attack and can significantly diminish the model's overall performance. In response, we present LAtent Concept Masking for robUStness (LACMUS), a novel perceptually-driven methodology that enhances DNN robustness without requiring prior knowledge about the adversarial contexts. We argue that DNNs' sensitivity to adversarial perturbations and distribution drifts stems from overfitting to non-common concepts within the dataset, leading to an over-reliance on specific learned instances and increased vulnerability. LACMUS addresses this by mapping high-dimensional data into a latent conceptual space to identify and navigate patterns of "non-common concepts" within the latent concept space. It then applies a concept masking strategy to selectively obscure data features, prompting the model to base its decisions on a wider array of information and thus enhancing its decision-making robustness. LACMUS distinguishes itself as a versatile, attack-agnostic framework that employs concept-wise augmentation to enhance robustness against a spectrum of adversarial, semantic, and distributional challenges. Our contributions include the development of a tool for robustness enhancement, a mechanism for mapping data to latent concept space, a strategy for identifying patterns of concept-wise misclassification, and a novel data augmentation module that leverages latent concepts. LACMUS is proven to enhance model resilience and generalization, even when training data is scarce, with experiments on MNIST, CIFAR-10, ImageNet, and CelebA supporting its effectiveness. We also provide augmented datasets to the research community, bolstering the robustness of models trained on them. 2977 2024 IEEE Symposium on Security and Privacy (SP)

We argue that DNNs' sensitiv- ity to adversarial perturbations and distribution drifts stems from overfitting to non-common concepts within the dataset, leading to an over-reliance on specific learned instances and increased vulnerability. LACMUS addresses this by mapping high-dimensional data into a latent conceptual space to iden- tify and navigate patterns of “non-common concepts” within the latent concept space. It then applies a concept masking strategy to selectively obscure data features, prompting the model to base its decisions on a wider array of information and thus enhancing its decision-making robustness. LACMUS distinguishes itself as a versatile, attack-agnostic framework that employs concept-wise augmentation to enhance robustness against a spectrum of adversarial, semantic, and distributional challenges. We also provide augmented datasets to the research community, bolstering the robustness of models trained on them. 1. Introduction Deep Neural Networks (DNNs), despite their outstand- ing performance in a variety of application domains, come with the caveat of weaknesses that may compromise their reliability. A notable vulnerability is the DNN's sensitivity to minute perturbations on the input data that fools the network to make incorrect outputs. These vulnerabilities manifest as sensitivities to adversarial examples [1], data distribution drift and semantic variations [2]-[4], leading to erroneous outputs. We highlight these robustness vulnerabilities in Fig- ure 1, showcasing the model's susceptibility to adversarial robustness (e.g., pixel perturbations), semantic robustness (e.g., changes in lighting), and distribution robustness (e.g., challenging samples cause distribution drifts). Ensuring ro- bustness against these factors is crucial, especially in critical applications such as autonomous driving, medical diagnos- tics, and financial services. Existing solutions for robustness, such as adversarial training, have demonstrated potential in constructing models resilient to adversarial perturbations [5], [6]. Notably, a key element of adversarial training's potency lies in effective data augmentation techniques to explicitly learn and fix “bugs” caused by variations. Research Gaps. Despite significant strides made in en- hancing adversarial robustness with the augmentation of adversarial examples, we identify four salient gaps that persist in existing adversarial training methodologies: • Gap 1. Attack-specificity. Current methods focus on spe- cific attacks, lacking efficacy against a broader spectrum of unseen attacks, even within the same category. We shall explore in Table 2 of Section 6, the robustness from adversarial training on FGSM [1] attack only has a little effect against other adversarial attacks such as PGD [5]. • Gap 2. Variation-specificity. While pixel-level perturbed data augmentation of adversarial training may fortify models against adversarial variations, they are ineffec- tive against other types of variations, such as seman- tic variations like lighting changes. A holistic solution that addresses both variations scenarios is conspicuously missing. We shall show in Table 2 of Section 6, the robustness from adversarial training on adversarial attacks only achieves minor robustness gains against semantic attacks like spatial rotation and distribution drifts. • Gap 3. Robustness and utility trade-offs . The enhance- ment of adversarial robustness comes at a notable cost to the performance on the original clean test set. The core of this issue lies in what is referred to as ‘problematic reg- ularization' [7]. This type of regularization leads to over- smoothed decision boundaries. Consequently, expanding the areas of indecision, where a model struggles to make clear, confident predictions. 2977 DOI 10.1109/SP54263.2024.00182 • Gap 4. Low-level Abstractions and Feasibility . Current adversarial training methodologies predominantly focus on pixel-level perturbations or layer-level manipulations, which correspond to low-level abstractions. These ap- proaches often overlook the structural attributes of images, underscoring the need for interventions at a more abstract level, such as the conceptual level, to enable effective interpretations. Additionally, constraints like proprietary restrictions can limit access to original samples for ad- versarial training, presenting feasibility challenges when working with a limited dataset. More details of existing works are provided in Appendix B. Motivation. We posit that a model's heightened sensitiv- ity to adversarial perturbations and data variations stems from overfitting on what we term ‘non-common concepts' within the dataset. Specifically, this overfitting arises when the model encounters an insufficient number of training samples relevant to complex concepts, like variations in lighting. In such scenarios, rather than learning general- izable patterns across these intricate concepts, the model memorizes the specific concept. This memorization leads to an over-reliance on these non-common concepts, in turn increasing the model's vulnerability to slight deviations or perturbations in the data that do not conform to its specific learned instances. Therefore, the overarching objective of robust data augmentation for adversarial training should be the enhancement of a model's proficiency in: (a) recog- nizing nuanced concept-wise representation; (b) identifying patterns of non-common concepts; (c) performing efficient adversarial training with regards to concepts. Traditional adversarial training methodologies often fail to address these aspects, as they largely operate within the realms of high- dimensional but low-level pixel space. The essence of LACMUS lies in its strategy to se- lectively obscure certain concepts within the data, thereby compelling the model to make accurate decisions based on the remaining, unobscured information. This method offers two significant benefits: firstly, it encourages the model to develop robust representations despite partial information occlusion; and secondly, it enables the model to ignore perturbations in the masked regions, effectively countering potential adversarial attacks. Design. The LACMUS methodology unfolds in four steps: i) Projection into Latent Concept Space. The initial step of the process involves converting high-dimensional data into a latent concept space using an encoder, aimed at distilling complex data into an abstract, concept-focused representation to capture its essential conceptual elements. ii) Identification of Non-Common Concept Patterns. The second phase entails a thorough analysis of the relation- ship between the data's conceptual representation and the model's classification outputs. By applying a concept mask to this representation and observing the subsequent changes in classification, we can effectively identify specific patterns, referred to as ‘non-common concept patterns', that critically impact classification decisions. iii) Augmentation of Conceptual Adversarial Samples. We generate augmented samples by strategically altering the concept representation based on the concept mask, followed by a reconstruction using a pretrained decoder. iv) Quantification of Robustness. Furthermore, LACMUS enables us to quantify the extent of perturbation required in the concept representation to alter classification outcomes. This metric serves as an indicator of a sample's robust- ness. Samples exhibiting lower robustness (i.e., those more susceptible to perturbations) are subjected to more inten- sive augmentation, thereby improving the model's resilience against variations in these specific concept areas. Contributions. This work presents a series of strategies and mechanisms that contribute to the landscape of model robustness. The primary contributions of our paper are enu- merated as follows: • Tool Creation. We introduce a tool to foster general robustness enhancement. This tool, centered on concep- tual augmentation based on latent concepts, attributes of being lightweight and attack/variation agnostic; capable of addressing both the adversarial perturbations and semantic variations in one shot. We also provide a measurement tool to evaluate the robustness of a sample. • Latent Concept Mapping Mechanism. A mechanism is applied to map data to a latent concept space, with informative and conceptual abstraction. This ushers in a transparent step forward in understanding the robustness characteristics of deep learning models. • Concept Discovery. We architect a comprehensive strat- egy to pinpoint the patterns of concept-wise misclassifica- tion. By leveraging latent concepts, we identify knowledge gaps that lead to vulnerabilities and biases in deep mod- els. These patterns then serve as conduits for robustness vulnerability to fool deep models. • Data Augmentation Module. We propose a data augmen- tation method that employs masking latent concepts. By suppressing occlusions on pivotal concepts, classification models can redistribute attention to other concepts. This approach offers a concept-wise and efficient solution to the longstanding robustness dilemma, by manipulating the low-dimensional, comprehensible latent concept represen- tation, thereby distinguishing our method from traditional adversarial training methods. • Efficacy. LACMUS stands out as a method capable of not only bolstering model resilience against adversarial attacks but also augments model generalization on seman- tic variations with reduced overfitting. Furthermore, we showcase the viability of LACMUS when only 0.5% of the original training samples are accessible for adversarial training, highlighting its feasibility even with severe data limitations. To validate LACMUS's efficacy, experimen- tation is conducted on benchmark datasets like MNIST, CIFAR-10, ImageNet, and CelebA. • Additional Dataset for Robustness Enhancement. Leveraging LACMUS, we contribute to the research community by offering augmented datasets crafted from prevalent public datasets. These augmented datasets are used to elevate the robustness of models trained or fine- tuned upon them. 2978
